questions.stem: What is meant by 'one mole' of a substance?

options.text: 6.02 x 10²³ particles of the substance (Avogadro's number)
The number of atoms that fit in one cubic centimetre
The relative formula mass of the substance in kilograms

questions.explanation: One mole of any substance contains exactly 6.02 x 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules, ions, etc.). This number is called Avogadro's constant. One mole of carbon atoms contains 6.02 x 10²³ carbon atoms, and one mole of water molecules contains 6.02 x 10²³ water molecules. The mass of one mole equals the Mr in grams.

questions.stem: How many moles of carbon dioxide (CO₂) are in 88 g? [Mr of CO₂ = 44]
questions.explanation: Moles = mass / Mr = 88 / 44 = 2 moles. One mole of CO₂ has a mass of 44 g (its relative formula mass in grams). Since we have 88 g, which is twice the molar mass, we have 2 moles. This formula (n = m/Mr) is one of the most important in GCSE chemistry.

questions.stem: What is the mass of 0.25 moles of sodium hydroxide (NaOH)? [Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1]
questions.explanation: First calculate Mr of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40. Then mass = moles x Mr = 0.25 x 40 = 10 g. One mole of NaOH weighs 40 g, so a quarter of a mole weighs a quarter of 40 g = 10 g.

questions.stem: A sample contains 3.01 x 10²³ atoms of iron. How many moles of iron atoms is this?
questions.explanation: Moles = number of particles / Avogadro's constant = 3.01 x 10²³ / 6.02 x 10²³ = 0.5 moles. Since Avogadro's constant (6.02 x 10²³) is the number of particles in one mole, half this number gives half a mole. The mass of iron is not needed here because the question gives the number of particles directly.

questions.stem: Which contains more molecules: 18 g of water (H₂O, Mr = 18) or 17 g of ammonia (NH₃, Mr = 17)?

options.text: The water sample contains more molecules
The ammonia sample contains more molecules
They contain the same number of molecules
Cannot be determined without knowing Avogadro's number

questions.explanation: 18 g of water = 18/18 = 1 mole of water molecules. 17 g of ammonia = 17/17 = 1 mole of ammonia molecules. Both samples contain exactly 1 mole, which is 6.02 x 10²³ molecules each. The masses are different but the number of molecules is the same because each sample is exactly one mole.
